evidence.claim: Socorro’s name began with the Piro pueblo of Teypana, whose people gave food and water to Juan de Oñate’s Spanish settlers in 1598.
evidence.quote: In June 1598, Juan de Oñate led a group of Spanish settlers through the Jornada del Muerto, an inhospitable patch of desert that ends just south of the present-day city of Socorro. As the Spaniards emerged from the desert, Piro Indians of the pueblo of Teypana gave them food and water.

evidence.claim: The Spaniards renamed that pueblo Socorro, meaning help or aid; the name later transferred to nearby Pilabó.
evidence.quote: Therefore, the Spaniards renamed this pueblo Socorro, which means "help" or "aid". Later, the name "Socorro" would be applied to the nearby Piro pueblo of Pilabó.

evidence.claim: The railroad arrived in 1880 and contributed to the growth of a town becoming a lead-and-zinc mining center.
evidence.quote: The New Mexico and Southern Pacific Railroad (a subsidiary of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe) arrived in July 1880, as it built south through the Rio Grande valley on its way toward El Paso. Its presence contributed to growth of the community, as Socorro also became a center of mining activity of lead and zinc:

evidence.quote: the brick dwellings which were built on and near McCutcheon Avenue in the 1880s and early 1890s using new materials and styles brought by the railroad and reflecting the prosperity of Socorro's mining boom.
